query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a phase‐selective recrystallization heat treatment to an as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will simultaneously increase its strength and ductility by optimizing the load-partitioning between a recrystallized, soft FCC phase and an intact, hard B2 (or intermetallic) phase.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., Al0.7CoCrFeNi or AlCoCrFeNi2.1) possessing a fine-scale lamellar microstructure consisting of a ductile FCC phase and a strong B2 phase.
generation.intervention: Implement a tailored heat treatment that induces selective recrystallization of the soft FCC phase while maintaining the integrity and connectivity of the hard B2 phase.
generation.conditions: Conduct the treatment at a temperature and time regime chosen to fully recrystallize the FCC phase without coarsening or altering the morphology of the B2 phase; processing should be performed under inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The engineered dual-phase lamellar microstructure with clean, robust phase boundaries that optimize strain partitioning.
generation.mechanism: Selective recrystallization homogenizes the ductile phase and sharpens the interface between the soft and hard phases so that during deformation, strain is more uniformly distributed. The intact B2 phase continues to provide high load-bearing capacity while the recrystallized FCC phase improves plasticity, thereby delaying crack initiation along weak interfaces.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, the treated alloy will exhibit an increase in yield and ultimate tensile strength (e.g., approaching or exceeding ~2 GPa) along with improved uniform elongation (e.g., increasing ductility to ∼35% elongation), achieving a superior strength-ductility balance.
generation.baseline: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with unmodified lamellar microstructure, which has limited ductility due to weak boundaries and premature crack propagation.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected only if the heat treatment successfully limits coarsening of the hard phase. Overaging or non-selective recrystallization that compromises the B2 phase connectivity may negate the benefits. The effect may also vary with slight compositional differences and processing variations.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility depend on precise control of the heat treatment parameters and alloy composition. There is uncertainty regarding the optimal temperature/time parameters required for different EHEA systems, and the interplay with any secondary precipitate formation is not fully established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of a selected eutectic high-entropy alloy: one set will remain in the as-cast state and the other will be subjected to the tailored phase-selective recrystallization heat treatment. Use controlled annealing parameters to selectively recrystallize the FCC phase while preserving the B2 phase morphology. Characterize the microstructures via EBSD and TEM to confirm selective recrystallization and phase integrity.
measurements: Yield strength and ultimate tensile strength via tensile testing
Phase morphology and recrystallization effectiveness via EBSD/TEM
Fracture surface analysis to assess crack initiation and propagation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant increase in both strength and ductility compared to the as-cast samples, or if the microstructural analysis reveals that the interface integrity or phase distribution has been compromised (e.g., excessive coarsening or non-selective recrystallization), then the hypothesis that phase-selective recrystallization simultaneously improves strength and ductility is falsified.

This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. Lamellar structures exist widely in various metallic materials such as A356 aluminum alloy (eutectic Al-Si) [], Mg-Al-Zn magnesium alloy (eutectic Mg-β-Mg17Al12) [], pearlitic steel (eutectoid cementite Fe3C + ferrite) [] and Ti-6.5 wt % Si alloy (eutectic Ti-Ti silicide Ti5Si3) [] and so on. Generally, a eutectic structure can exhibit high strength and ductility by combining a hard phase and a ductile phase. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have become a new research frontier in the metallic materials community; they offer a wide range of microstructural tunability from simple single-phase condition to complex eutectic mixtures. Compared to conventional metallic materials, HEAs hold distinct characteristics: (1) high-entropy effect, (2) sluggish diffusion effect, and (3) severe lattice distortion [,]. Excellent ductility is crucial not only for shaping but also for strengthening metals and alloys. The ever most widely used eutectic alloys are suffering from the limited ductility and losing competitiveness among advanced structural materials. Here we report a distinctive concept of phase-selective recrystallization to overcome this challenge for eutectic alloys by triggering the strain hardening capacity of the duplex phases completely. We manipulate the strain partitioning behavior of the two phases in a eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) to obtain the phase-selectively recrystallized microstructure with a fully recrystallized soft phase embedded in the skeleton of a hard phase. The resulting microstructure fully releases the strain hardening capacity in EHEA by eliminating the weak boundaries. Our phase-selectively recrystallized EHEA achieves a high ductility of ∼35% uniform elongation with true stress of ∼2 GPa. This concept is universal for various duplex alloys with soft and hard phases and opens new frontiers for traditional eutectic alloys as high-strength metallic materials.
